content: Surgical face masks were initially designed to trap and filter droplets containing microorganisms that are expelled from the mouth and nasopharynx of healthcare workers during surgical procedures. This was intended to protect the patient from potential contamination. However, surgical masks may also inadvertently contribute to wound contamination. For example, improper wearing of the mask or air leakage from the sides due to inadequate string tension can lead to contamination. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the use of disposable surgical face masks by the surgical team during clean surgical procedures reduces the incidence of postoperative surgical wound infections. In December 2015, as part of the seventh update of this review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. Additionally, the bibliographies of all relevant publications were reviewed. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of disposable surgical masks with no mask use during surgery. Two independent reviewers extracted data from the included studies. Ultimately, three trials involving a total of 2,106 participants were included in the analysis. None of these trials demonstrated a statistically significant difference in surgical wound infection rates between the groups that used masks and those that did not. No new trials were identified in this latest update. Based on the limited evidence available, it remains unclear whether the use of surgical face masks by the surgical team has any effect on the rate of surgical wound infections in patients undergoing clean surgical procedures.
